data.description: Build a full LLM-powered interactive CLI experience for RiotPlan that mirrors the MCP/Cursor workflow. The current CLI commands don't match the MCP tools/prompts/resources. Need to create commands like explore_idea, build, gather evidence, print plan info, and execute - all backed by an interactive LLM chat session (via OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). The LLM needs access to tools similar to what Cursor provides (file reading, lookups, command execution) so it can do the same kind of deep exploration and planning work.

data.content:
The main entry point into RiotPlan right now is via MCP in Cursor, which works well, but RiotPlan was also envisioned as something usable outside of an IDE, from the command line. The current CLI commands don't resemble the MCP tools/prompts/resources at all. 

What's needed: commands that match the most frequently used entry points into the RiotPlan experience - explore_idea (to start or develop an existing idea), building a plan once shaped, gathering evidence, printing plan info, and executing a plan.

The core complication: idea exploration in Cursor relies on a powerful LLM on the other end of a conversation. For CLI, we need to instantiate an interactive chat session using OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Additionally, in Cursor the LLM isn't just conversational - it can read files, lookup information, and run commands. The CLI needs to build out a similar set of tools for the LLM to use during the interactive experience.

Overall vision: use riotplan outside of MCP such that the CLI manages a dedicated LLM experience with tool access.

data.description: Existing AI provider infrastructure in RiotPlan codebase
data.originalQuery: What existing AI/LLM infrastructure exists in the riotplan codebase?

data.note: The current AI usage in RiotPlan is one-shot generation: you feed artifacts in, get a plan out. The CLI experience needs a fundamentally different pattern - an interactive conversation loop where the LLM can call tools, ask questions, and iterate. This is the core architectural challenge.

The kjerneverk monorepo already has execution packages (execution-anthropic, execution-openai, execution-gemini) that handle direct API communication. The 'agentic' package likely contains tool-use infrastructure. These are building blocks for the interactive CLI experience.

data.constraint: Must work with existing API keys: OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (and potentially GOOGLE_API_KEY) - no new auth infrastructure needed
The CLI LLM experience needs tool access similar to what Cursor provides - file reading, file lookup, information search, and command execution - not just a bare conversational interface
CLI commands should map to the most frequently used MCP entry points: explore_idea, build plan, gather evidence, print plan info, execute plan - not a 1:1 mapping of all 36 MCP tools
Must leverage existing execution packages (execution-anthropic, execution-openai, execution-gemini) and the agentic package in the kjerneverk monorepo

data.question: What does the 'agentic' package in the monorepo provide? Does it already have tool-use loop infrastructure (tool definitions, execution loops, response parsing) that we can reuse for the CLI agent?
What tools should the CLI agent have access to? At minimum: read files, search files, read plan artifacts. But should it also be able to run shell commands, write files, or make git operations?

How should the interactive terminal experience work? A REPL-style chat? A rich TUI with markdown rendering? Plain text with streaming responses? How do we handle tool-use visibility (show the user what the LLM is doing)?
Should each CLI command (explore, build, execute) launch its own agent session with a tailored system prompt (matching the MCP prompts), or should there be one generic 'riotplan chat' command?

How do we handle the MCP prompts in CLI context? The explore_idea prompt, for example, has detailed instructions about when to call which tools. Should the CLI agent get the same prompt as its system message, with RiotPlan tools wired in as LLM tool-use functions?
What about cost management? Cursor users don't pay per-token for the LLM. CLI users calling APIs directly will incur costs. Should there be token budgets, model tier selection, or cost warnings?

Should CLI sessions be resumable? If I run 'riotplan explore my-plan' and have a 20-turn conversation, close the terminal, and come back later with the same command, should it pick up where I left off? How does conversation history persist?

data.description: Agentic package assessment - tool infrastructure exists but no agent loop
data.originalQuery: What does the agentic package provide for building an interactive CLI agent?

data.description: Execution packages assessment - need extensions for tool-use conversations
data.originalQuery: Do the execution packages support tool-use conversation loops?

data.note: Critical finding: The agentic package has ToolRegistry, tool format conversion, and security/sandboxing, but NO agent loop. The execution packages can call LLMs but can't pass tool definitions or handle tool-use conversations. Building the CLI agent requires work at both levels: extending execution packages to support tools+streaming, AND building the agent loop that orchestrates multi-turn conversations with tool use.

data.content:
On tool access scope: User wants to recreate Cursor's capability. Notes that people may be overestimating what Cursor actually provides - it has a robust allowlist mechanism but the tools themselves are straightforward. Points to CodePuppy (https://github.com/mpfaffenberger/code_puppy/tree/main/code_puppy/tools) as an example of the kind of tools needed.

On command structure: "explore", "build", "execute" are a good start. Also wants a generic "chat" command.

On execution packages: Yes, this plan should include the foundational work of extending execution packages to support tool-use conversations.

On session persistence: The plans themselves should be the persistence layer. But keeping track of the chat transcript like we track prompts would be useful for returning to it after the fact. The plan is the state, the transcript is the record.
data.context: User responding to exploration questions about scope, command structure, execution packages, and session persistence
data.speaker: user

data.description: CodePuppy tool analysis - reference implementation for CLI agent tools
data.originalQuery: What tools does CodePuppy implement that we'd need for a similar CLI experience?

data.note: The user is right that the tool set is straightforward. CodePuppy's core is just 6 tools: list_files, read_file, grep, edit_file, delete_file, run_shell_command. The complexity isn't in the tools themselves but in the agent loop that orchestrates multi-turn conversations with tool use. CodePuppy uses pydantic_ai which handles this natively. RiotPlan (TypeScript) needs to build this loop.

Session persistence approach: Plans ARE the persistence. Chat transcripts should be stored alongside plan artifacts (similar to how .history/prompts/ already captures conversation context). The plan's state (IDEA.md, SHAPING.md, STATUS.md) survives across sessions. The chat transcript is supplementary record, not the primary state.

Command structure decision: Four primary commands - 'riotplan explore [path]', 'riotplan build [path]', 'riotplan execute [path]', 'riotplan chat [path]'. Each launches a purpose-built agent session with a specific system prompt derived from the corresponding MCP prompt. The 'chat' command is a generic fallback for ad-hoc interactions.

data.question: CodePuppy uses pydantic_ai which provides the agent loop natively. For our TypeScript implementation, should we: (a) use the Anthropic/OpenAI SDKs directly and build a minimal agent loop, (b) use an existing TypeScript agent framework like Vercel AI SDK, LangChain.js, or similar, or (c) build it into the @kjerneverk/agentic package as the missing ConversationBuilder/StrategyExecutor that was planned but never implemented?

Should the RiotPlan CLI agent have write access to non-plan files? During 'explore' you mainly read and add to plan artifacts. During 'execute' the LLM might need to write code, run tests, edit source files. Should write tools be scoped to the command type?

data.content:
User wants to keep the agent loop implementation in-house rather than using Vercel AI SDK or similar. Motivation is partly to demonstrate that this isn't something you need third-party dependencies for. Believes it should be relatively easy to implement.

User also questions why streaming would be difficult in the execution packages - asking what the actual complexity is.
data.context: User deciding on build-vs-buy for agent loop, questioning streaming complexity
data.speaker: user

data.note: Decision: Build the agent loop in-house within @kjerneverk/agentic. The loop is genuinely simple (~20 lines of core logic). The agentic package already has ToolRegistry, format converters, and LLMClient interface. This also completes what was originally planned for that package (ConversationBuilder, StrategyExecutor). No need for Vercel AI SDK or similar.

Streaming is straightforward, not a Phase 2 concern. Both Anthropic SDK (client.messages.stream()) and OpenAI SDK (client.chat.completions.create({stream: true})) provide async iterables. The current providers just never needed streaming because they did one-shot generation. Adding executeStream() to the Provider interface is ~30-40 lines per provider. Should be included in the foundational work, not deferred.

data.content: User asking a critical architectural question about how the CLI agent differs from the MCP/Cursor model. In Cursor, the calling model (e.g., Opus 4.6) does the thinking — RiotPlan just provides tools (accounting/organization) and prompts (telling the model what to do). The model in Cursor calls RiotPlan tools but also has access to Cursor's own tools (file read, grep, shell, etc.). When running from the command line, is the CLI agent doing the same thing — is it the same architecture where one model does the thinking and RiotPlan provides tools?
data.context: User probing the fundamental architectural difference between MCP model and CLI model
data.speaker: user

data.note: Critical architectural insight: The CLI and MCP paths share the same fundamental architecture — one model does the thinking, RiotPlan provides plan-management tools and prompts, and the host (Cursor or CLI) provides environment tools (file read, grep, shell). The CLI just needs to provide everything that Cursor + MCP provide together: the model hosting, the agent loop, the prompts as system messages, the RiotPlan tools as LLM tool-use functions, AND the environment tools that Cursor normally provides. The underlying tool implementations can be shared.

data.question: Should the RiotPlan tool implementations be refactored to have a shared core that both the MCP tool handlers and the CLI tool-use functions call? Or should the CLI tools call the MCP tool implementations directly (they're just async functions under the hood)?

data.description: Architecture comparison - how CLI agent mirrors the Cursor MCP model
data.originalQuery: How does the CLI agent architecture compare to the Cursor/MCP model?

data.content: User confirms the architecture matches their vision. Adds an important observation: because we're spinning up the LLM ourselves and defining the tool set, we have MORE control than in Cursor. We can prevent the model from editing plan files directly — it can only modify plans through RiotPlan's structured tools. This is a strict, enforceable boundary that's actually harder to achieve in Cursor where the model has access to all of Cursor's native tools.
data.context: User confirming architecture and noting the control advantage of CLI over MCP
data.speaker: user

data.note: Important advantage of CLI over MCP/Cursor: the CLI has stricter tool control. In Cursor, the model has all of Cursor's native tools (file editing, shell, etc.) PLUS MCP tools — the MCP server cannot restrict what Cursor's tools do. In the CLI, we define the complete tool set. If we don't give the model a write_file tool during 'explore', it physically cannot edit files — it can only modify plans through RiotPlan's structured tools (idea_add_note, idea_add_evidence, etc.). This makes plan integrity enforceable at the tool level.

Tool scoping per command becomes a design feature: 'explore' gets read-only file tools + RiotPlan idea tools (no file editing). 'build' gets read-only file tools + RiotPlan build tools. 'execute' gets full file tools (read, write, edit) + RiotPlan step tools + shell. 'chat' gets everything. This is precise, intentional control that MCP can't enforce.

data.description: CLI control advantage over MCP - enforceable tool scoping and plan integrity
data.originalQuery: Capture the CLI control advantage for later documentation

data.constraint: No backwards compatibility requirement with existing CLI commands. The old CLI (amend, amendments, analysis, elaborate, feedback, generate, render, verify) can be replaced entirely. Just make the new interface work.

data.note: This is freeing. The existing CLI was built around an older "analysis → generate" workflow that predates the lifecycle model. Rather than trying to evolve those commands, we can start fresh with the commands that match how RiotPlan actually works now: explore, build, execute, chat. Plus utility commands like status, step list, etc. that don't need an LLM session.

data.name: Layered Bottom-Up
data.description: Build in strict dependency order across the monorepo packages. Phase 1: Extend execution packages (add tools parameter to Request, add executeStream(), update Anthropic and OpenAI providers). Phase 2: Build the agent loop in @kjerneverk/agentic (ConversationManager, AgentLoop that orchestrates LLM calls with tool use, streaming support). Phase 3: Define the tool sets — both RiotPlan tools (wrapping existing MCP tool implementations) and environment tools (read_file, list_files, grep, run_command). Phase 4: Build the CLI commands in riotplan (explore, build, execute, chat) that wire together the agent loop with the appropriate tools and system prompts. Each layer is independently useful and testable. The execution packages become useful for any project, not just RiotPlan. The agentic package becomes a real agent framework.
tradeoffs: Pro: Each layer is independently useful — execution packages and agentic become reusable across projects
Pro: Clean separation of concerns — easy to test each layer in isolation
Pro: The execution package improvements benefit existing one-shot generation too
Pro: Agentic package finally gets its planned ConversationBuilder/loop infrastructure
Con: Longest path to a working CLI — you don't get a usable command until all layers are built
Con: Risk of over-engineering lower layers before knowing exactly what the CLI needs
Con: Touches 4+ packages in the monorepo which means more coordination and more publish cycles
Con: Could spend weeks on infrastructure before seeing a single riotplan explore session work
assumptions: The execution package extensions are generally useful beyond this project
The agentic package agent loop will be reused by other tools
Clean layering is worth the upfront cost
The existing MCP tool implementations can be cleanly wrapped as LLM tool-use functions

data.name: Vertical Slice
data.description: Build one complete command end-to-end first, then replicate the pattern. Start with `riotplan explore` as the vertical slice — it's the most common entry point and exercises all the layers. Build just enough in each layer to make explore work: minimal executeStream() for one provider (Anthropic or OpenAI, whichever is preferred), a minimal agent loop in agentic that handles multi-turn tool-use conversations, the explore-specific tool set (read_file, list_files, grep + RiotPlan idea tools), and the explore CLI command with the system prompt. Once explore works end-to-end, extract patterns and build the other commands (build, execute, chat) which follow the same structure but with different tool sets and prompts. Extend to the second provider after the first works.
tradeoffs: Pro: Fastest path to a working riotplan explore — could be usable within days
Pro: Real usage informs the design — discover what the agent loop actually needs by building a real command first
Pro: Avoids over-engineering — build only what's needed, not what might be needed
Pro: Easy to demo and validate early — show the explore experience, get feedback, iterate
Con: First slice might not generalize cleanly — patterns discovered during explore might not fit execute
Con: Second provider (OpenAI/Anthropic) added later, so initially locked to one
Con: Less clean layering — might need refactoring when adding the second and third commands
Con: The agentic package might end up with explore-specific assumptions baked in
assumptions: explore is the right first slice (most common, exercises all layers)
Patterns from explore will mostly transfer to build/execute/chat
One provider is enough to validate the architecture
Refactoring after the first slice is acceptable and expected

data.name: Pragmatic Layered
data.description: A hybrid that builds layers but with a working command as the forcing function. Phase 1: Extend execution packages with tools parameter and streaming (both Anthropic and OpenAI — this is straightforward work that's well-scoped). Phase 2: Build the agent loop in agentic AND the explore command simultaneously — let the explore command's needs drive the agent loop's API. The agent loop gets built to serve explore, but designed with the other commands in mind. Phase 3: Build the environment tools (read_file, list_files, grep) and RiotPlan tool wrappers. Phase 4: Wire up explore end-to-end. Validate it works. Phase 5: Build remaining commands (build, execute, chat) using the now-proven agent loop and tool infrastructure. This approach does the foundational work first (execution packages, since it's well-understood and small), but lets the explore command shape the agent loop design rather than designing the loop in abstract.
tradeoffs: Pro: Foundational work (execution packages) done right and for both providers from the start
Pro: Agent loop design is informed by real usage (explore) but not limited to it
Pro: Working explore command relatively quickly — after phases 1-4
Pro: Clean enough layering that packages are independently useful
Pro: Second through fourth commands (build, execute, chat) are faster because the infrastructure is proven
Con: Slightly slower than pure vertical slice for the first working command
Con: Still requires judgment calls about what to generalize vs what to defer
Con: Phase 2 (simultaneous agent loop + explore) requires discipline to not over-couple them
assumptions: Execution package extensions are well-understood enough to do for both providers upfront
The explore command is a good-enough proxy for what the agent loop needs
Discipline to keep the agent loop general while building it alongside explore
The other commands (build, execute, chat) are structurally similar enough to benefit from a proven pattern

data.reason: Best balance of doing foundational work right (execution packages for both providers upfront since the scope is clear) while letting real usage (the explore command) drive the agent loop design. Avoids both over-engineering in the abstract and painting into a corner with a single slice.
Approach selected (Pragmatic Layered). Building plan manually since AI generator not available in this session.
